title: Memento mori, gently
hook: remembering death helps us live well
tomorrow: what's the difference between hope and wishful thinking?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: at the hour. Every Hail Mary keeps the last hour in view. Today, the old habit of keeping it there on purpose.

Some people keep a chart of their life in tiny squares, one per week, and shade one in each Sunday night. It sounds grim, a countdown on the wall. The idea is the opposite: seeing the squares makes the week ahead feel precious. The Church has its own version. On Ash Wednesday, a thumb of ash crosses your forehead, and one of the lines said comes from Genesis: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return."
screen: `A LIFE IN TINY SQUARES.` → `GRIM, OR PRECIOUS?` → `A THUMB OF ASH.`

segments.voice: So the question: does remembering death make life smaller, or bigger? The Catholic answer is bigger. Sirach puts it in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin." Not to scare you; to sort you. Remember the end, and the grudge you're keeping shrinks. The Latin is memento mori: remember you will die. Saint Benedict, among his tools for good works, tells his monks to keep death daily before their eyes. Some paintings of Saint Jerome put a skull on his desk, next to his books. And for Catholics the end isn't a wall. The raised body, heaven, the saints: remembering death is remembering where you're going. Here's something a neighbor tradition shares. The Buddhist Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here; but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." Two traditions, one discovery: remembering death makes people gentler. And one honest difference. The Dhammapada's frame is impermanence: all things pass, and seeing that clearly frees you. The Catholic frame is a God who raises the dead. Same habit, different horizon.
screen: `SMALLER, OR BIGGER?` · `REMEMBER THY LAST END.` · `THE DHAMMAPADA: QUARRELS CEASE.` · `SAME HABIT, DIFFERENT HORIZON.` · then, large: `REMEMBER, AND LIVE.`

segments.voice: Choose the next hour of your day. Name the one thing most likely to steal it: the scroll, the worry, the grudge. Decide now what you'll do when it shows up, and what you'll do with the hour instead. Then rest in the quiet. This hour won't come twice.
Memento mori. Latin for remember you will die: not to frighten you, but to sort what matters.
Keep this one: remember, and live, because the end shows you what the hour is for. See you tomorrow.
